review:
You play as Alan Wake, a writer battling a sinister dark force using light as a weapon, trying to recover his missing wife and unravel the mystery of his own story. This is a horror thriller.

✅ Very dark atmosphere
✅ Strong, twist-filled narrative
✅ Good mix of action and horror
✅ Well-written plot and characters that keep us in suspense until the very end
✅ Graphically, the game looks phenomenal; in my opinion, it didn't need a remaster. It's from 2012 and is still impressive by today's standards (only the grass and bushes look bad).
✅ DLC included in the price (two special episodes that continue the main storyline).
✅ Varied locations (forests, campsites, a town, a power plant).
✅ Alan Wake's voice reading pages from the manuscript.
✅ Very good idea regarding equipment. We have a flashlight that blinds our enemies with its light, and additional items such as flares, flashbangs, and rocket launchers that provide light.
✅ Good weapon selection. We only have a revolver and two shotguns. I can't imagine having an AK-47 or M4 in this game.
✅ Very enjoyable shooting mechanics.
✅ Variable weather and atmospheric effects add to the immersion.
✅ Car driving motif has also been added.
✅ Great sound design that changes the tone of the game, keeping us on the edge of our seats. It fits perfectly with the atmosphere of the game.
✅ Dream sequences and hallucinations add an extra layer of mystery and unease.
✅ The artist's struggle with his work is a recurring motif throughout the game.
✅ Good character controls and fluid movement.
✅ Good menu options, including FOV adjustments.
✅ The game is divided into 6 episodes, plus 2 additional ones with great music after each one.
✅ The episodic structure gives it the feel of a great TV show.
✅ For fans of collectibles, the game has plenty to offer (106 typewritten pages, 100 coffee thermoses, knocking over 12 pyramids of cans, finding 30 hidden chests, 11 radio programs, 14 television programs, 25 signs, 10 alarm clocks, 6 cardboard silhouettes, and 10 games from the Night Springs series). There's plenty to explore, though I'm not a fan of this kind of content, so it's a plus for those who enjoy it.
✅ The game’s length is perfect; it's neither too short nor unnecessarily stretched out with an artificial, boring storyline.
✅ Three difficulty levels to choose from: easy, normal, and nightmare.
✅ No noticeable bugs.
✅ Very good price for such a high-quality game.
✅ Frequent save points throughout the game

✅❌ The game is linear, so, as with every linear game, everyone has to decide for themselves whether they enjoy that or not.

❌ Very weak puzzles. For example, the generator can be activated by double-clicking at the right moment. They could have introduced more complex puzzles or controlled them differently.
❌ Alan Wake's stamina is too low. He can run about 20 meters before getting tired, which quickly becomes frustrating for the player. Sprinting depletes stamina far too quickly.
❌ Jumping animation looks terrible.
❌ Poor enemy variety.
❌ The flashlight battery drains too quickly. The game could have allowed for longer battery life at the expense of fewer batteries scattered throughout the story.
❌ I don’t understand why the developers don’t allow players to start on “Nightmare” difficulty during their first playthrough.

[h1]Alan Wake Review[/h1]

[hr]
[h1]Overview[/h1]
Alan Wake has been sitting on my list for a long time, and I finally decided to play it. I also went for all the achievements, and overall I had a phenomenal experience.

It is obviously an older game and some parts show their age, but the story, characters, atmosphere, and simple gameplay still hold up really well. It is not perfect, especially when it comes to repetitive combat and the insane amount of collectibles, but I am really happy I finally played it.

[hr]
[h1]Story and Characters[/h1]
The story was easily one of my favorite parts of the game. My first playthrough took me around 12 hours with collectible hunting, and I stayed interested pretty much the whole way through.

Without spoiling anything, the game slowly introduces you to Alan Wake, Bright Falls, the Darkness, and everything strange happening around you. As you progress, you gradually understand more about who these people are and what is actually going on.

I really liked Alan as a character, and his narration adds a lot to the experience. It genuinely feels like you are playing through a story as it is being told. Barry is also great and brings a lot of personality to the game.

The voice acting is excellent overall, and the narration, characters, and story all work together really well.

[hr]
[h1]Atmosphere and World[/h1]
The atmosphere is fantastic.

Alan Wake is mostly linear, so you always have a pretty clear idea of where to go. You spend a lot of the game around Bright Falls and its surrounding forests, usually at night with your flashlight and whatever weapons you have.

The dark forests, ambient sounds, music, and constant feeling that something could appear around you create a really good atmosphere. The soundtrack was especially memorable for me.

Visually, it obviously looks like a game from the Xbox 360 era, but that never bothered me. Performance on PC was also excellent in my experience. I had no crashes, noticeable bugs, or major FPS problems during my playthrough.

[hr]
[h1]Combat[/h1]
The combat is simple but fun at first.

Most enemies are protected by the Darkness, so you first have to burn it away with your flashlight or another light source before you can properly damage them. You get weapons like the revolver, shotguns, hunting rifle, and flare gun, along with flares and flashbangs.

The light mechanic feels fresh in the beginning, and the game slowly introducing more tools helps keep things interesting for a while.

The problem is that the basic combat loop barely changes.

Towards the end I got tired of constantly stripping the Darkness from enemies and then shooting them, especially when the game started throwing large groups at me over and over again. At some points I just wanted to run past combat completely.

That is also difficult because Alan's stamina is terrible. He gets tired extremely quickly, and enemies usually catch up unless you use flares or another way to slow them down.

The combat never became terrible, but by the final episodes it was definitely more repetitive and annoying than it was at the start.

[hr]
[h1]Collectibles and 100% Completion[/h1]
This was easily my least favorite part of Alan Wake.

There are way too many collectibles. You have 100 coffee thermoses, 106 manuscript pages, supply chests, radios, TVs, signs, can pyramids, and more. On top of that, 15 manuscript pages only appear on Nightmare difficulty.

If you are going for 100%, use a guide.

The game tracks what you collect pretty well, but actually finding everything is the problem. Constantly checking a guide, leaving the main path, grabbing something, and checking what comes next completely ruins the pacing.

Some episodes took me over two hours because I was making sure I did not miss anything, and with this many collectibles, missing one somewhere in a long episode is extremely annoying.

I like collectibles in games, but Alan Wake simply has too many. If you are only here for the story, this is barely a problem. If you are going for all the achievements, prepare yourself.

[hr]
[h1]The DLCs[/h1]
Alan Wake has two story DLC episodes, The Signal and The Writer, and I honestly did not enjoy either of them very much.

They continue the story and introduce a cool mechanic where shining your flashlight on words can make objects, weapons, lights, and paths appear. It is a neat idea, but it was not enough to make me enjoy the levels themselves.

Both DLCs felt strangely constructed compared to the main game, almost like custom levels built using Alan Wake's mechanics and assets. They are not very long and their collectibles are nowhere near as bad, but if I was not going for the achievements, I probably would not have bothered finishing them.

The Signal in particular was rough for me.

[hr]
[h1]Late Game[/h1]
The final parts of the main game also started feeling stretched out.

The story was still interesting enough to keep me going because I wanted answers, but gameplay-wise I felt like I had already seen almost everything the game had to offer.

By Episode Six especially, the repetition became noticeable. There was more combat and more enemies, but not enough new ideas to keep the gameplay feeling fresh.

[hr]
[h1]What Works[/h1]
[list]
[*]Great story and memorable characters
[*]Alan and Barry are both excellent
[*]Fantastic voice acting and narration
[*]Excellent atmosphere, soundtrack, and sound design
[*]Simple but satisfying light-based combat
[*]Bright Falls is a memorable setting
[*]Very smooth PC performance in my experience
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]What Falls Short[/h1]
[list]
[*]Combat becomes repetitive later on
[*]Too many enemy encounters towards the end
[*]Alan's stamina makes running away frustrating
[*]Way too many collectibles for 100% completion
[*]Collectible hunting hurts the pacing
[*]The DLCs were disappointing for me
[*]The final episodes start feeling stretched out
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Alan Wake is a brilliant game, and I am really happy I finally gave it a chance.

If you enjoy story-focused games, horror themes, dark atmosphere, and interesting characters, there is a lot to love here. Alan is a great protagonist, the narration is excellent, and Bright Falls has an atmosphere that still works incredibly well.

The combat gets repetitive, the collectible grind is ridiculous if you want all the achievements, and I could have lived without the DLCs. But the main game was still a great experience.

Absolutely worth playing.

It’s not a positive review, it’s a neutral one. I can’t recommend this game and I can’t say it’s not worth playing either.

It started great. The atmosphere reminded me of Twin Peaks and The Twilight Zone – a mystery, a small town with a complicated history. The soundtrack in this game is on point, so every song matched the environment really well, one of my favourite parts of Alan Wake.
I was playing on Steam Deck, and the game looked really nice on a smaller screen. Of course, it’s old now, but nothing immersion-breaking.

And this is where the combat comes into question. It’s an extremely repetitive use light - shoot the enemy cycle. But let’s say the devs wanted the light mechanic to be the main focus. Okay, fair, but then make the game shorter. Why is it so long if the majority of the game you’re just running through the samey woods, fighting exact same enemies? Especially chapter 3, it was a slog.

The game also has these weird difficulty spikes where, out of nowhere, it just throws dozens of the most annoying enemies at you. Considering how janky the dodge is, it’s not a fun time.
Honestly, after the 4th chapter I just wanted it to be over.

The story is what carried the game for me, what made me stick till the end. Very entertaining, a unique premise. It has both serious moments and cheesy ones. Barry wrapped up in Christmas lights was genuinely so funny to me. And fighting on the rock stage with music blasting felt awesome.

The ending of Alan Wake felt kinda rushed. You’re running back and forth for hours just to get a 3-minute cutscene that resolves everything. However, there are two special episodes (DLC) that explain the ending and what happened after.

“The Signal” was pretty much the same thing as the main game but with more difficult enemies and frustration. Didn’t enjoy this one.
“The Writer” is much better. It’s focused on Alan’s mind, has a surreal and distinct from the rest of the game feeling to it. I’m glad I played it.

Now I’m intrigued by Control and Alan Wake 2, but I’m definitely not coming back to this one.

Short version:

Pros:
+ Movie/Book references
+ Gorgeous vistas and detailed, lived-in environments
+ Splendid atmosphere
+ Gripping storyline with interesting characters
+ Satisfying gameplay
+ Voice acting is great

Cons:
- Lip syncing is laughable
- Combat does not evolve after a while
- Driving controls could be better

“Long” version:
[u]Alan Wake[/u] is an atmospheric third-person shooter “horror” game. You play as the aforementioned Alan Wake and you must uncover the secrets that plague the town of Bright Falls.
It was developed and published by Remedy Entertainment.

I played this a while ago but never really finished the DLC. I decided to come back to it a few months ago and 100% it. It was one of my first Steam games and I have always wanted to complete it. I have reviewed it years ago for a website and, as it turns out, it still holds up and the score remains the same, even after 7/8 years.

The storyline is great. You plunge into a very interesting mystery after a solid introduction and you must figure out what happened to your wife, Alice, after she went missing. There are many twists and turns, but I really enjoyed the overall take on a story that could be too predictable and shallow if mishandled. Luckily, even side characters get some development and the game does not really feel like it has levels; it has episodes instead, so it basically feels like a very thought-out TV series. Episodes feel long and engaging and they swiftly build up into an epic finale.
I will not delve into any particular plot-threads, as I want to avoid spoilers, but I can say that I found myself caring for characters I hated at first, I was invested and felt for them whenever something unfortunate happened and that I would also love for them to return in the now-announced sequel.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=366106681

With the story out of the way, let us talk gameplay.
While you do an awful lot of exploring, it is not the most demanding part of the game. It is very simple and you do not usually have to time jumps or make harrowing escapes. Alan is an average-Joe so he cannot leap great distances nor can he run great distances without running out of breath.
You can occasionally drive around small map sections. The controls are not sharp enough for it to be enjoyable, though. I found myself crashing into things way too many times; whenever I wanted to back up and try again, I would get frustrated and would most likely go on foot in the end.
What I enjoyed the most about exploring this world, however, were the landmarks and the amazing world building. I will explain more about it under the graphics section of my review.

You will go up against enemies called the Taken during combat sections. They are covered in a thick layer of shadows and you must get rid of it to make them susceptible to damage.
For this purpose, you carry a torch – you must shine your light on enemies in order to make their defenses drop faster; this, however, requires batteries and a very “fun” resource management dynamic is introduced (at least on harder difficulties).
After the enemies lose their defenses, you are free to shoot them. You do this with a plethora of guns – revolver, hunting rifle, shotgun, etc. You also get two more weapons which are a bit more “exotic”; the flare gun and the flashbang. These simultaneously damage and light up an area, disposing of most enemies in a single hit.
You can also dodge enemy attacks, triggering a super stylish slow-mo effect.
While I found the combat to be a lot of fun, I feel like most people will find it a bit “boring” after a while. You see, you quickly get introduced to all the weapons and game mechanics. [u]Alan Wake[/u]’s idea of a challenge is to introduce enemies that take more bullets to kill or with a bigger shadow shield, but even that gets introduced quickly. After that the game just sends bigger waves of enemies that required little to no adaptation and it sort of grows stale.
Do not get me wrong, as I said, I liked it; I found the combat to be enjoyable, but it sure is repetitive.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=395556015
Graphics are up next.
This game is a looker. Even all these years later. It is not so much the graphics that are great (even though I still think they most definitely hold up), but the art direction and the overall atmosphere of it. [u]Alan Wake[/u] is filled with gorgeous, moon-bathed vistas and sprawling forests. The warm and inviting town of Bright Falls feels lived-in and it is quite glorious to witness it getting “invaded” by the Taken.
Lip-syncing, however, is not good. While you can ignore it for the most part when characters are talking, more dramatic scenes that have characters emote (screaming, for example) can be ruined by the laughable animations.

The game features great voice acting. Some of it might sound cheesy at first but I do feel it fits the overall mood of the experience. Main characters are expertly voice-acted and most side-characters are fine. Enemies have a very creepy filter that makes them sound ethereal and menacing.
Guns sound impactful, which makes the combat more fun and dynamic.

There are plenty of references to horror movies and books – collectibles, name drops, story beats, etc. It is great and used sparingly.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=395555822
Even after all these years, I truly enjoyed Alan Wake. I feel like it falls a tiny-tiny bit short of being amazing – not because of its age, but because of some pacing issues when it comes to gameplay and some janky facial animations and vehicle controls. But that is about it when it comes to negatives; on the other hand, you get a great story with respectable character development, plot twists and an overall enjoyable combat system that features creative mechanics. There is also plenty of eye-candy with strong art-direction.

A classic.

Final score: 8.5 out of 10.

[/list]	

[h1]REVIEW[/h1]
[i]”Nightmares exist outside of logic” – Stephen King[/i]

[b]Alan Wake[/b] is an extremely enjoyable third person action-adventure/survival game with a very story-driven experience and the theme of a psychological thriller. It is a very cinematic game, with a lot of dialogue and cutscenes. So if you need constant action, you won’t find it here; but if you enjoy games that feel a lot like movies-you-control, this is a great pickup.

The backbone of this game is the excellent narrative, which is well-executed and well-acted. The main story arc is mysterious, intriguing, and suspenseful.  And the voice acting is quite convincing, which is critical for a game this heavily story-driven. But my personal favorite aspect of [b]Alan Wake[/b] is the development of the various characters. Video games sometimes have great stories, but often they lack the depth of character development one may find in other mediums of storytelling, like books, TV, or movies. The way this game was produced, though, it is easy to feel the connection with the characters and immerse yourself in their personalities.

The graphics, animations, effects, and soundscape all work in concert to create an extremely engaging atmosphere that reinforces the strong narrative. The gameworld looks great and you can feel the heavy atmosphere of the creepy little village that acts as the story’s setting.  This vivid and intense setting allows the entirety of the game to be entertaining; even slow plot points remain amusing due to the immersive ambiance.  If you are into immersion, [b]Alan Wake[/b] is definitely the kind of game you want to play with headphones on, lights off, and no interruptions.

But looking past the engaging narrative and atmosphere, you will find that the actual gameplay is also pretty decent. The controls are mostly solid, albeit a little clunky— but it is the kind of clunky that is purposefully imposed to adhere to the paradigm of the scary/survival genre.   And there is an interesting dynamic involving shadows and illumination from which all action/combat is derived and that affords the game a charming uniqueness. There are also a lot of collectibles that provide further lore/backstory and add an additional dynamic to the total gameplay. Be warned however: the collectibles system can break the immersion of the game at times because you’ll have to sidetrack to find them during intense moments in the storyline.

In short, [b]Alan Wake[/b] is a great experience.  It may not appeal to those who want constant action from their games, but for those who enjoy cinematic, narrative-driven games, then this will be great to consider trying if you haven’t yet.  The dark psychological-thriller theme is easy to find intriguing and the gameplay, while not innovative, has a unique charm that is gratifying to experience.

I first played Alan Wake on Xbox 360 over a decade ago but only got through the first couple chapters. I enjoyed it at the time but for whatever reason I put it down and never came back to it.

Alan Wake is a great game that has a terrific story. The presentation is great with it structured like a TV show with distinct  episodes and recaps at the beginning of each one.
The combat get a little repetitive but I was always wanting to find out what was going to happen next. 
I highly recommend Alan Wake if you like any other Remedy game or are a fan of action/thriller games.

The atmosphere is the best part—creepy, tense, and really well done. Using light to fight enemies is a cool idea, though the combat can get a bit repetitive after a while.
Overall, it’s a great pick if you enjoy story-focused games with a thriller vibe.

So, a few months back I decided to play the [b]Alan Wake[/b] series, Alan Wake, 2xDLCs & American Nightmare. I went a little retro and wanted to play some games that others said were good, and that were stored in my gaming queue years ago, and never played. (I know yuou have them, too) :D  

[h1]So, What is the Alan Wake game about?[/h1]
Alan Wake is the main protagonist in this game. He was a bestselling author who had been struggling to write anything for two years due to a case of writer's block. His wife, Alice Wake, brought him to Bright Falls to try and recover his creative/writing flow, which of course sends Alan's life into a spinning tale of Light -vs- Darkness. Also, he is the protagonist of the DLC's (Special One: The Signal & Special Two: The Writer) and the stand-alone Alan Wake's American Nightmare. Alan must figure out a way to defeat the darkness within him. Oh... and save his wife.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1302987796
[h1]Alan's Background[/h1]
As a child, Alan had a fear of the darkness and he was afraid of monsters hidden in it. He would fight sleep to the bitter end out of fear. His mother gave him an old, used broken-off light-switch dubbed [spoiler]The Clicker[/spoiler]. Every time he would flip the switch on it, a supposed magical light would turn on and the monsters would vanish. Over time, he conquered his fear of darkness.

At some point he met Barry Wheeler and they became close and true friends. Soon after, Alan became interested in writing. He became an avid reader of Stephen King and other horror writers, and then started writing his own stories using his vivid imagination. Alan rose to becoming famous, but as he wrote more and more books, he gained a constant following of annoying fans and interfering paparazzi. He grew a temper and then came under significant heat after he punched a journalist who wouldn't leave him alone. 

Alan married a photographer named Alice. They lived together in a New York City apartment three years prior to the Bright Falls incident. But as he finished his Alex Casey series, he began to suffer once more from writer's block and insomnia. There was trouble in their marriage, and Alan kept on coming home drunk from parties. The two got into many fights, with Alan constantly frustrated at his inability to write anything at all.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1345252894
Alan drives to Cauldron Lake with Alice, arriving at Bird Leg Cabin. The couple are awed by the beauty of the scenery surrounding the lake, along with how gorgeous the house is. Alan settles in and contemplates on how great the cabin will be for his vacation. But when he goes inside after looking around the island, Alice reveals a surprise to him. A typewriter with pages in the study of the cabin. Alice tells him that she thinks that the change of scenery and a psychiatrist named Emil Hartman might help him write again. 

Alan is furious and storms out of the cabin with a flashlight. But as soon as he walks out, the lights in the cabin go out and he hears his wife screaming from inside. Alan runs in and catches a glimpse of Alice drowning in the lake. Alan dives in to save her.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1351982816

[b]Now, YOU need to play the game to find out what happens next!!![/b]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Alan Wake is described by Remedy as "the mind of a psychological thriller" and "the body of a cinematic action game" put together. The game's creators hold that the game does not belong squarely in the survival horror video game genre. I totally agree.

Gameplay consists of using a Keyboard/Mouse or a Controller. I used a controller when playing this game. I just found it easier to move around. You control Alan Wake and in the game, the "darkness" takes over humans, animals and objects. These enemies, dubbed the "Taken", are murderous shadows that attack Wake, wield weapons that  range from mallets and knives to shovels and chainsaws. They vary by speed, size, and the amount of damage they can take, and some can teleport between short distances. Besides the Taken, the player must combat flocks of possessed ravens and animated objects. When enemies are close, Alan can perform a slow-motion cinematic dodge maneuver. This was fun and exciting, I think.

If you are a Keyboard and Mouse PC player and want to become more adapt with a controller, play this game! Fighting and running throughout 90% of this game has allowed me to become comfortable with the Controller. I did not have any issues with the controller hooked to my PC while playing this game.

[h1]DLC Notes[/h1] I found that about 45-60% of the people I talked with about Alan Wake, didn't know the DLCs were included. They are accessed via the game menu as episodes. Play "Special 1: The Signal" first and "Special 2: The Writer".

[olist]
    [*]The Signal: Continuing on where the main game finished, Alan finds himself outside the diner (at night) in Bright Falls..  which quickly changes to daytime. Entering the diner, a surreal déjà-vu dream of the events play out similar to when Alan first arrived, with everything eerily familiar but out of place. Going deeper into the DLC, warning messages plays out, a new type of invisible Taken appears and hound Alan throughout the story. Alan is slowly panicking and slowly losing himself saying "there’s no way out...I need to get out of here'!!"
    [*]The Writer: This is the eighth and final episode in the game. The episode finds Wake in strange circumstances, now fully aware of the thing that opposes him, he must survive one increasingly nightmarish situation after another. The Signal depicts Alan is trapped within himself. Instead of fighting the darkness or his book, he is now fighting himself, as his projections try to kill him within his mind. I found it repetative, but totally fun! 
[/olist]

[h1]Game Thoughts[/h1]
I had a blast with this game. It met my expectations of an Action, Adventure game set in an atmosphere of constant state of a psychological thriller. The game has an intense atmosphere, deep and multilayered story, and aged combat sequences [PC Game released in 02/2012]. I found it very entertaining.

- Great Story Endings, not any loose endings that I can recall when playing Game + DLCs... :D
- Graphics are Very Good for its age. The rustic scenery was fantastic!
- Great atmosphere and story, IMO,
- Awesome soundtrack,
- Boss fights were pretty challenging (for me) and i had to learn how to fight and evade while running backwards,
- For me, 46 hrs to complete base game and DLCs + Item Collections 
- 1st Playthrough achievement progress: 52 of 67 (78%) achievements earned
- Not very repayable unfortunately, 
- Steam Notice: The base game Alan Wake is no longer sold on Steam.
- At the time of this writing, certain resellers are still selling the game.. e.g. "G_2_A".

I'd add it to your collection while supplies last.
- Great game!

INTRODUCTION:
Alan Wake is a survival horror third person shooter developed by Remedy Entertainment on the Xbox 360 in 2010 which slowly made its way to the PC 2 years later. It only took 48 hours for the game to surpass the development cost after their PC release.

You play as (duh) Alan Wake, a writer who channels Stephen King, who, while on vacation with his wife in a sleepy mountain town, soon find themselves in the center of a supernatural phenomenon that threatens to engulf the town in darkness.

PROS:
+ Combat: - The combat in itself is not original since it plays like your regular Resident Evil third person shooter, however, it does spice things up by making all the enemies invulnerable until you strip away the 'darkness' that protects them using any source of light (flashlight, torch, flares etc.)

+ Atmosphere: - The town and the surrounding mountains and forest are dark, mysterious, foreboding and generally hostile. Not a great place for a vacation but a great place for a survival horror action game. Great lighting is what really made the atmosphere stand out.

+ Story: - (Also a CON, see below) The game boast a good story line that keeps players wondering what's going to happen next with its unique story telling mechanic. The mystery is deep and the characters within it are well written.

+ Sound: - This would normally go to Atmosphere but I think it deserve its own bullet point. Voice Acting is great, sound effects are well implemented and the musical score are suited to the general theme.

CONS:
- Horrendous Facial Animations: - The character models are good, textures are nice, but the lip syncing and general facial animations are awkward and painful to look at.

- Story: - (Also a PRO, see above) If the player has ever read a Stephen King book or seen a movie with a Stephen King book as its basis, then you can easily see where this game HEAVILY takes its inspiration. So heavy in fact that it can be seen as unoriginal.

- Too Much Forest: - This is kind of a personal gripe I have with the game. It has way too much forest sequences that makes me kinda hate nature. The forest sequences are nicely done, but if repeated way to many times, it looses its charm.

CONCLUSION:
GREAT GAME. If you're looking for a third person Survival Horror experience and you're one of the disappointed Resident Evil fans, then Alan Wake is a good alternative. It delivers a clever new mechanic to the third person shooting aspect that does not involve chest high walls or massive explosions. Though the re-playability might not be great, Alan Wake still brings a lengthy adventure that makes your money's worth.

Alan Wake is a psychological thriller developed by Remedy. It won't take too long to realize the plot, setting, characters and the overall vibe are heavily inspired by some of the most popular TV shows and novels out there. Some of obvious inspiration include The Twilight Zone, Twin Peaks, X-Files, Lost, Stephen King and more. There are just hundreds of pop-culture references, easter eggs and funny gags throughout the game. There are also many real-life sponsored product placements for Verizon, Ford, Xbox, Microsoft, Energizer and Lincoln Motors xD which some of you may not liked but I did not mind them as they added a realism to the game's world. The story is written and directed by Sam Lake best known for his works on Max Payne, Quantum Break and recently released Control.

One of the most interesting thing about the game is that it's crafted like a TV season in episodic format something that a lot of people don't mention here on Steam. The game is divided into 8 episodes; After the first episode's exposition each that follows ends with a cliffhanger, fades to a title screen as songs from the game's excellent licensed soundtrack play, and then transitions into a plot recap as the next begins with Previously on Alan Wake narration. You know the drill........

Gameplay is kept simple. Light keeps the darkness away, your flashlight is the most important weapon to drive away the zombie like enemies (they're called Taken). Combat is straight forward but requires precise thinking. Ammo and flares are limited. Use them wisely, if you're surrounded its wise to run and save the bullets. Since this is a Remedy game you'll be in a treat for a kickass experience.

Yeah!!!! Highly recommend buying the entire Alan Wake collection on a sale. Keep in mind that this game is not for everybody. Psychological thriller and cinematic action game in one.

Alan Wake is an action-adventure game developed by Remedy Entertainment and published by Microsoft Studios.

Meet Alan Wake, an author of a bestselling crime fiction series, suffering from a writer's block. He and his wife Alice travel to the small mountain town of Bright Falls for a short vacation, which quickly turns into a nightmare as his wife gets kiddnaped, forcing Alan to save her and figure out what is going on before it's to late.

Alan Wake is structured like a thriller television show, it contains multiple plottwists, cliffhangers, and is seperated into episodes with each having a recap of what happened (and what will). Thankfully it has no ad breaks.
It's a linear journey, with few larger sections where you travel using a vehicle, with simple objectives on your way you need to complete in order to progress further. 
You will make your way through Bright Falls and areas surrounding it while fighting off creatures, animals and objects corrupted by "Darkness", vulnerable to light and bullets.

Light has a lot of power in Alan Wake and you need to use it in order to survive. Your main source of it, a flashlight, allows you to eliminate all enemies, including human shadows called Taken, who have shields made from darkness. You need to expose them by burning the shield down and then use firearms to eliminate them.
Light also helps you discover clues and hidden stashes of supplies.
Flashlights run on batteries, which can be collected throughout the game, just like ammunition or other resources.
Game also features different light-based weapons and accessories like flare gun or flashbangs, allowing you to quickly eliminate groups of enemies, and enviromental light sources such as streetlights, provide you a safe haven where you regenerate health faster and enemies can't reach you.

But when they can, you need to be careful. Taken come with dfferent melee weapons and in different sizes, but besides more health and stronger shield there is not much of a change in their approach. They also come from different directions. When they get close, Alan can dodge their attacks, if you get hit, you lose health, which slowly regenerates when you don't recive damage, or if you are in safe haven.

Outside of combat you can explore the locations for additional supplies, or collectibles!  Main collectible in the game is a manuscript, or rather pages of it, spread across the game. Fun part is, you won't collect every page by playing the game once, not only that, some pages are restricted to highest, hardest difficulty called "Nightmare", adding more replayability and challenge to those who want to visit Bright Falls once again. Rest of collectibles can be called "side collectibles'. Those are 100 coffee thermos flasks, television sets, radios airing talk from local radio station, plus text signs giving additional lore. So there is plenty of times to interract and collect! 

Besides mentioned "Nightmare" mode game also features additional 2 Bonus Episodes which follow Alan Wake after events from main game, so play them after finishing main story first. 

While game plays out like a typical action-adventure title, it stands out thanks to fantastic, mysterious atmoshpere which with a mixture of episodic tv show format constantly keeps you on your toes awaiting additional twists, enemies, and other dangers hiding in dark woods, abandoned towns or empty streets of the town. 

Due to limited enemy variety combat becomes slighty repetitive at the end of the game, when you have meet all the types of enemies.  
Alan Wake features occasional "boss fights" which also do not add any variety to the combat and focus on same light-flashing as any other fight, but simply they take longer, so those could also be better. 
My main annoyance lies in ending, maybe developers went a biiit too far with copypasting the structure of tv show. Main story ends with a cliffhanger, which nowadays is fixed by those two additional episodes, but here is a twist, those also end on cliffhangers. It would be alright if we got a sequel but that didn't arrive yet. So story with all those twists at the end feels slightly dissapointing due to ending. 
There are also few smaller elements that could be tweaked. 
Checkpoint system is ridiculous, feels like there is one after every fight and every minor interaction. Just way too many of them, making the game feel easier than it is, in specific moments it even allows you to skip combat and run straight forward to get to next checkpoint. AI once in a while gets crazy as enemies sometimes get stuck behind items while allies are killing machines. 

Didn't have any issues with game performance as Alan Wake runs smooth, it's a well optimized title. 

Game's score was composed by Petri Alanko, and soundtrack features few songs made by band "Poets of the Fall". Some are used for end credits in each episodes (like in tv shows) while some you can hear when travelling. Both of those types add more of the "tv thriller show" vibe.

Even with all those smaller and bigger issues Alan Wake is probably the best thriller game out there that doesn't disguise itself as a survival horror title. Great atmoshpere, fantastic format and enjoyable combat make it a game worth your time. 8/10!

It has taken me 7 1/2 years to finish playing Alan Wake. I bought it in 2012, ancient history, right? On an older rig, the gameplay felt janky and perhaps I shouldn't have started out on hard difficulty. I kept being axed by that one Taken enemy that I didn't see coming up behind me and Alan Wake's notorious lack of running stamina meant he kept falling to thrown weaponry before he could start that generator or reach the safety of that just-out-of-reach light.

But there it has sat, silently rebuking me, always at the top of my alphabetical Steam library... like a book classic I always meant to read rather than skim the Cliffsnotes. So, I quickly reinstalled it at the beginning of this week and late last night (very late last night) I got through the darkness and finally closed the book on the last chapter. It was well worth it.

Alan Wake is an old school game: it naturally has more in common with Remedy's more renowned original Max Payne than with anything else I've played. It's a solid narrative experience, with enough depth to merit a replay, and enough gameplay to encourage achievement hunting (both in-game and for Steam achievements). I want to try a run where I don't shoot anything and reach each checkpoint through adroitly deployed flares to delay enemies that snap at my heels. Alan Wake is solid. I wish I had played it sooner.

Having finished my game late at night I dreamed Alan Wake as I slept. It was one seriously phantasmagoric night. Alan Wake leaves an impression. The game still looks good in 2019. Its textures are beautiful. Only Alan Wake himself, appropriately, has aged, with dated facial animation and a corny, self-aggrandizing seriousness that reflects an age when people read books more and took writers seriously.

It wasn't until I activated a TV screen to see a recording of Alan on a late night talk show, hamming it up with the host, who urges the two people out there who haven't read Wake's latest book to do so, that I felt the immersion break-- even Stephen King doesn't appear on any talk shows now (at least none that I've ever watched) even though he is still one of the most prominent writers in America. His moment has passed and it's all new writers of topical non-fiction that get the air time.

Similarly, Alan Wake's moment has passed. As good as it is, I doubt there would ever be a remake. Max Payne was able to muster the energy to relocate south of the border, but Alan Wake has got nowhere to go. He's written his last book. It's a good one though: it's well worth revisiting. If you haven't yet discovered it, then it's your turn, reader, to put away the Cliffsnotes, and seek the light.

Alan Wake is a psychothriller game based on supernatural powers. It shows how powerful darkness really is. The game is set in a rural town called Bright Falls in Washington state, USA. Alan Wake is a professional writer from New York City who decides to go on a vacation in a small town. However, his vacation turns into a nightmare as he is attacked by possessed beings known as the Taken. Wake’s wife is apparently kidnapped from their cabin located in a nearby lake, encouraging Wake to look for her in the wilderness. The game is spread across six episodes that feel like a TV show.

As Alan Wake looks for his wife, manuscript pages are scattered in each episode. The manuscript pages flesh out the story of the suspense Mr. Wake is going through, although he does not remember writing it. There are many strange plot twists such as crazy things happening shortly after reading about them in his manuscript pages. Wake is a disturbed man and this sets up effective storytelling.

The gameplay is mainly in the night when darkness rears its ugly head. There are a few daytime scenes, but it is best that there no more daytime scenes. Otherwise, too many daytime scenes would have taken away the moody feel of the game. There are many scary encounters with the Taken, who are armed with knives and other projectiles ready to kill Wake. You can evade these possessed humans by running from their attacks, creating a cool cinematic dodge. Every time you enter a new store or turn a corner you feel anxious about who or what will come after you. The Taken are vulnerable to light, so that is when your flashlight, flares, and flashbang grenades come into play.

Aiming at the Taken is required, but shooting at them without aiming a flashlight at them to remove their strength of darkness is a waste of valuable ammo. As soon as you take away their darkness, you can shoot them with your conventional weapons like a revolver, shotgun, or hunting rifle. Ammo is not very plentiful, so it is important to use your ammo wisely. You can choose to run away from them so that you can reach the next safe haven, a place where strong light is projected onto the ground. The Taken do not dare enter the light for fear that they will be killed.

When the Taken are not attacking you there are possessed objects such as barrels, cranes, bulldozers, etc. These possessed objects seem to be from the famous movie Poltergeist. You must use Wake’s flashlight or flares to disintegrate possessed objects, as they are vulnerable to light and cannot be shot. I found it quite scary to see a bulldozer suddenly turn on and chase me while no one was inside driving and a few Taken were attacking. This is when your battle skills are tested to see how good you are with your flashlight, flares, and flashbang grenades. Your flashlight loses battery power and must be recharged. The limited battery power adds to the suspense of having to insert a new battery while the Taken and/or possessed objects are threatening to kill you. It is also quite unsettling when flocks of ravens suddenly descend upon you from the sky and the only way to eliminate them is by using light sources. The only problem I have with the combat with the Taken is that it may feel a little repetitive when heading toward the end of the story in episode 6.

The graphics of Alan Wake are still neat on the PC. Bright Falls looks gorgeous in the day during rare daytime scenes. The night looks detailed enough when looking at an abandoned farm that looks decrepit. The graphics make this small town look authentically rural. I found a few graphical glitches in some indoor settings, but they are rare and superficial.

After completing the main story, you can choose to play the DLCs, including The Signal and The Writer. The DLCs are definitely worth playing since they expand on the main story. The Signal and The Writer both feel even creepier and more bizarre than the main story. It was particularly scary when suddenly, not one, but two monster trucks were chasing me in The Signal DLC with no one inside either monster truck.

I highly recommend Alan Wake for its well written horror story that translates into spooky atmosphere for the gameplay. It is a creepy game that does not let up and keeps the combat tight and intense until the very end for the main game as well as for the DLCs. I firmly believe that the DLCs, although short, are worth playing and retain the creepy atmosphere.

My Score: 8.5/10

Even after all these years Alan Wake holds up as an excellent game. It has a great formula to it where you have to break down an enemies shield with light before you can actually harm them as well as you being able to be healed by areas of bright light. It seems simple but it works well and there are a variety of weapons to use as well as different light sources to use. The game does a great job of introducing various weapons and game play mechanics in a natural way. The story is top notch as is the voice acting and music. Remedy has always been fantastic at these elements and even if I didn’t know they made Alan Wake I would have guessed based on the music choices and voice acting talents used as they have Remedy’s finger prints all over them. The game has a great flow to it, trying to mimic a TV show with great success. The game also delivers side plot detail in creative ways such as TV shows being displayed on TV’s; finding pages of the manuscript you have written and listening to radio shows. There are driving segments and luckily they are pretty decent which, given that Remedy had never done any driving game play before, should be praised. The graphics are overall above average for it’s time but isn’t without fault. Object details in the world; water; lighting; trees and fog are all great. Clothing detail is a mixed bag. Face and car detail is decent. Ground detail is mediocre. Fire detail is poor. Remedy has always done little details well. In Max Payne they had footprints in the snow and shell casings on the ground where here in Alan Wake they have things such as used flares being on the ground after which is a nice little touch. There are a couple segments where you are alongside an AI companion while they fight off the “taken” coming after you and overall the segments aren’t bad but the aim of your companions sure are. One other bit I found odd was that when the dark presence controls somebody they speak in a very strange way almost as if they were in a drug induced haze but nobody in the game seems to notice this strange behaviour. There are some awesome moments of game play in Alan Wake that were very memorable. I’ll single one out: having to survive a swarm of taken on a music stage with rock music blaring as your buddy works the pyro effects and lights was simply awesome. The difficulty curve is handled well, often being challenging but never feeling sadistic.

	I played Alan Wake on Linux using Valve’s Proton. It crashed on me one time during game play. I also had issues with audio not playing in various cut scenes that was solved by using the launch command "WINEDLLOVERRIDES="xaudio2_7=b,n" %command%" which solved any audio issues I had. There are 3 AA settings; 4 AF settings; 2 SSAO settings; a v-sync toggle and 7 other graphics options. There is an FOV slider but there are no numbers on it. Alan Wake is a writer who hasn't been able to write anything new for several years. In search of inspiration and solitude, Wake and his wife come to a small town where, during the course of the plot, unknown people kidnap Alan’s wife, and then over the phone demand Wake’s latest novel. The problem is that he does not remember at all how he wrote it, but he regularly finds pages of a work in which he clearly recognizes his handwriting. An additional inconvenience is created by the fact that everything described on the pages found tends to come true within the next few minutes. The game's narrative is divided into episodes, and the gameplay in the game is quite simple: we go from point A to point B, dealing with obstacles along the way. These could be enemies, closed doors or puzzles. I liked the game, although the plot is a little clichéd, there is a thriller and drama here, and the simple gameplay is not very boring. Critically speaking, this game is terrible. I heard other people describe it as "Best 6/10 game I've ever played" and I wholeheartedly agree.

The gameplay loop is basic and it overstays its welcome by about 6 hours. The protagonist mostly walks alone in a dark corridor and keeps commenting on every single thing that happens. Combat is sluggish, with about 6 types of enemies repeated in different quantities throughout 10 hours of gameplay. It doesn't really get better because no matter whether you shoot enemies in the head or their pinkies, they take the same amount of damage. 

The voiceacting honestly just sucks, especially for the protagonist. He never, ever changes the tone he's speaking at, no matter the situation. He wishes his wife "Good morning" with the same emotion as he later expresses when he wants to torture her kidnapper. In most scenes, it seems no one was giving voice actors any direction and they didn't do retakes for obviously fumbled lines.

The writing feels like an inconsistently self-aware B-movie. You get these insane scenes like an FBI agent shooting at you for seemingly no reason, even though you're next to a civilian, as the FBI agent shouts the names of other famous writers at you. And he changes the name he shouts EVERY TIME. I honestly do not understand people who unironically praise the writing of this game, because it feels like they must've never even seen the inspirations the game draws from. The constant references to Stephen King and The Twilight Zone, in my opinion, drag the game down because it points out how much they just wanted to emulate something without having the skill to do so.

But honestly, at least I had quite a lot of fun with how terrible it is. The writing is campy, sometimes it is self-aware, sometimes it's just stupid. Tha game certainly hasn't aged well and I'd hardly consider it one of the greatest games of all time. Yet, it is kinda funny and fun at times.

If you ever come across someone who believes that video games aren't art, just show them this game. I genuinely enjoyed this game from start to finish. I mean sure, the first ten minutes of gameplay felt weird to play in 2025: besides the graphics, the camera angle required getting used to at first, there was one or the other graphical bug or system freeze. But keep in mind, this game was released 15 years ago. 

Other than that, Alan Wake is a game that just excels in it's story telling and gameplay. The combat, although it gets heavily criticized, is one of it's major selling points to me. It gets frustrating from time to time, you might have to repeat the same section several times (looking at you episode 2), but it is so clever and unique, that I just can't hate it. You have to strategize, set priorities, make use of whatever your environment offers. What's even more funny to me is that only after finishing the game, did I find out that I have been playing this on hard difficulty the whole time.

The story telling? Chef's kiss, kept me hooked the whole time. TV shows, radio stations, manuscript pages that tell you how the story will continue? So many ways of narration that just keep you engaged, there is no other game that made me go "this is such creative story telling" this many times while playing like this game did. The price is already good enough and it's a steal on sale, totally worth it. I will be playing the DLC episodes, American Nightmare and Control next. Now after finishing the main story, I wonder how much better Alan Wake 2 must be then, considering how impressed I was already by playing the first game.

Update: I can highly recommend playing the DLC episodes. The first one was alright, nothing special in my opinion but the second one was great! It requires a lot of platforming but the implementation of walking into a sort of hamster wheel that depicts story moments is quite incredible. American Nightmare certainly is a nightmare as a game but it has some fun combat.

If you're reading this now, 10 years after this game's release, wondering whether it's worth a try - then the answer is yes.

After finishing Control, I was really keen to know about the Bright Falls Altered World Event in that game - and Alan Wake, being part of the same connected universe, is the chronicle of that.

Storyline wise, its sublime. Told in a episodic style, imagine something somewhere between 70% of Stephen King's mythos, Twin Peaks, X-Files and one of the better SCP Foundation entries and you have this. Taking place during a holiday to cure his writer's block, Alan and his wife Alice take a break up in the Pacific Northwest, in a quaint little town where nothing is as it seems. Game on. I won't go into any more detail then that because the story is a treat.

Graphically - you're not going to mistake this for a game made last year, but it still looks great. The lighting effects, the presentation, the Darkness, it's all here. Every so often you'll see a blurry texture but for a game as old as this, its very easy on the eyes. Sound is the same - voice acting and music are simply top class. There'll be points, lost in unsettling darkness that the whole presentation comes together to form a very creepy tale.

If there's a downside - realistically, while the Fight With Light mechanic (shine light on opponent, wait until shadow burns off, gun down/explode) works really well and doesn't really get old, the rest of combat is a chore. This divides into two aspects - Alan and his weapons.

Alan is allegedly a normal writer in his mid-30s, but in what I'm presuming is an attempt to drive this home by the devs, he handles like 90-year-old with arthritis. I'm not kidding, *everything* this guy does feels slower or less effective then you'd otherwise expect. Sprinting? he burns out after a 3 seconds. Jumps are pathetic. Reloading and switching guns can lead to nearly breaking your keys on your keyboard as the guy somehow manages to turn the most basic actions into a saga - which can be frustrating when you're surrounded by murderous possessed lunatics.

The second aspect is the guns, which are about as bland as it gets. Bright Falls appears to be the only place in the USA where semi-automatics aren't a thing. When the highlight of your arsenal is a pump-action shotgun, you know you're not exactly in for satisfying combat. 

Overall though, its not enough for it to be a problem. The base version of the game on Steam comes with both the DLC episodes which collectively form an epilogue, and they're as worth a play as the rest of the story.

If you like horror, get this. If you like a great story, get this. If you're a fan of Control - then I'd still recommend it, even if the combat isn't a patch on that game, as its great to see the crossover.

Let's get one thing out of the way: If you're a creative type, especially a writer of any persuasion, Alan Wake is worth a playthrough just for the subject matter, namely the nature of dreams, the unconscious, and the creative process, and how they are all tied up in each other. Any professional fiction writer will tell you that they often don't know where their "ideas" come from -- they might as well just come straight out of the proverbial ether, and to anyone else it sounds like superstitious mumbo-jumbo. But the truth is, it often really does come out of left field, left field being that ocean of subconscious impulses and images that is constantly roiling in everyone's heads. A writer's job is paying attention to those images when they do show up, when most people can comfortably ignore them, and that makes it a tricky business. That's the gist of what Alan Wake deals with, and if anything, it's worth it to see what the game devs have to say about it.

Is it a GOOD story? Well. That is entirely up to your interpretation of the events in the game. And I'll mostly leave it at that. I'll give some of my impressions in no particular order: If you like the show [i]LOST[/i], you'll like this. If you like David Lynch's stuff, you will like this, particularly for some of the music and very obvious homages to things like [i]Twin Peaks[/i], [i]Blue Velvet[/i] and perhaps [i]Lost Highway[/i]. That is to say, if you want things to make sense in a linear way, forget it. It's actually a little bittersweet to play through this if you are a big fan of Lynch, because while Alan Wake is very very obviously a love letter to the "weird stuff happening in a little town" genre, and it really does nail some of the spooky imagery that Lynch is known for, the characters and the dialogue fall disappointingly flat. It's a very rough imitation of the unforgettable dialogue of [i]Twin Peaks[/i], [i]Blue Velvet[/i], etc. I can't fault them that much for that, because at least they tried. Enough of that.

Gameplay is pretty technically tight with satisfying, challenging gunplay mixed up with light-source mechanics -- you weaken things with your flashlight, and then blast them. It's fun and keeps you on the edge of your seat most of the time. But, and this just may be my low tolerance for the same damn thing over and over, there are many times later in the game where you wish you could just get it over with. The pacing is a little annoying and predictable at times; when you would appreciate a chance to just wander around in the more story-oriented areas, suddenly you're back in the gauntlet of enemies running through the nighttime forest. And there is a LOT of nighttime forest. You've never seen so many trees! But they certainly look pretty. One of my biggest gripes would have to be the fact that the game occasionally does not follow its own rules, which inevitably leads to some frustrating reloads. The enemies will sometimes cheap-shot you, for example falling on you while you're in the middle of opening a chest; most of the time you cannot break out of certain "cinematic" moments fast enough and it will screw you fairly mercilessly. Thankfully reload times are fast and the checkpoints for the most part are plentiful and logical. Just minor annoyances when it comes down to it.

It's a fun ride for the most part. I wish I could say that "this is, excuse me, a [i]damn[/i] fine cup of coffee," but for several reasons it's just a pretty good cup of joe. You take what you can get, though!

Alan Wake is a combination of survival horror and psychological thriller. It looks, plays, and feels a lot like an episode of Twilight Zone, from which the game overtly draws a lot of inspiration. Alan Wake is *not* an action game, but there are combat sequences which feel forced, repetitive, and unnecessary. 

[b][u]The Good:[/u][/b]

* Interesting and compelling story, although it is cliche at times. I get the light/dark motif and its importance to the theme - but it is as old as sin and you don't need to cram it down my throat!

* The game runs great on PC; it is hard to tell this is a console port. I originally played the game on console and I think I now prefer it on PC.

* Fantastic graphics and atmosphere. The town of Bright Falls feels like a real town in its own fictional universe with its own radio stations, TV programs, and billboard advertisements.

* The game is frequently only $3-$5 (up to 90% off!) during Steam sales, which is one of the best deals I have seen for a AAA title on Steam.

[b][u]The Bad:[/u][/b]

* The player is asked to press F5 quite often to read manuscript pages. However, once done reading the manuscript, the player is given the option to (a) cancel, or (b) return. These two options are fairly ambiguous, and I more than once chose the "cancel" option, which required me to navigate through several menus to actually get back to the game.

* Uninteresting "collectibles" mechanic - why am I supposed to collect these coffee thermoses if I have no idea what they do or how to keep track of them? Why is someone hiding them in horrible places, such as behind this large sign that happens to have an invisible wall next to it?

* The combat is unique but completely uncomepelling: you must first shine a flashlight on an an enemy for perhaps 3-4 seconds before your bullets will do any damage. In practice, this mechanic is the least-interesting portion of the game. I ended up dreading combat sequences as they distracted from the game's only strong-suit: the plot.

* Inconsistent ammo/resource management feature. At times I was constantly at maximum capacity, and at other times I was avoiding entire mobs of enemies to conserve ammo. If I was ever low on ammo, I could always spend 5-10 minutes backtracking to pick up ammo that I left earlier due to being at maximum capacity the first time around. This is entirely flawed game design: either give the player a larger capacity for ammo, or don't give them the ability to go back and pick up ammo they missed. Making the player go backwards at a snail's pace is NOT a feature.

* Awkward controls limit Alan's mobility. Why can I jump over some knee-high ledges, but not small logs that are about ankle-high?

* The "extra episodes" are horrible. My first death occurred because I walked into some floating text a few times....

[b][u]The Ugly:[/u][/b]

* Horrible check point system. There are no save games, just checkpoints. If you barely survive an enemy encounter with only 1 bullet left and happen to end up at a check point, that's it, there's no retrying that fight to see if you can land a better outcome. That one bullet is all you have now, and you now have to either start the entire game over or try running through the rest of the chapter without fighting any enemies (which is virtually impossible if there are more than 2-3 enemies at once.)

* Outside of the fantastic plot, the game, at its core concept, is a hallway with uninteresting obstacles in the way. By the end of chapter 2, you will begin to ask yourself how many more repetitive trails in the middle of the woods you will have to travel to reach the end of the story (spoiler: a lot more).

* Even though I have touched on the plot being fantastic so much, there are some huge plotholes. If the monsters are afraid of light, why didn't Alan buy a much bigger flashlight before he went venturing around at midnight? If a non-monster person wanted to meet Alan, why did he set the rendevous time to be at night when the monsters are out and he knows it is unsafe? There are also MANY more plotholes that would be spoilers if I typed them here. Also, as in the Bioshock games, if you don't collect all the manuscript pages (which are often somewhat hidden), you are liable to miss entire sections of the plot.

[b][u]The Verdict:[/u][/b]

Oh wow, this is... actually one of my favourite games ever now. I've known about Alan Wake for a while but didn't know anything about it, and certainly didn't expect it to be this good.

[b] Before I get into the review, an [u] IMPORTANT WARNING: [/u] [/b] after you complete the 6 main Episodes, the game will roll the credits, but there are TWO EXTRA EPISODES that the game DOESN'T TELL YOU ABOUT. You have to actually go to the Episode Selection menu and you will see Special 1 and Special 2 under the other 6 main Episodes. These are not inconsequential side episodes, they are a DIRECT CONTINUATION of the main story and THE TRUE ENDING IS IN THEM. I cannot stress this enough, based on the achievements 27% of players have finished the main episodes, but ONLY 8% have played the Special Episodes, the others didn't see the ending of the story. This is structured this way because these Special Episodes were paid DLC when the game was on Xbox, but are included for free on the Steam release. Why they didn't add a warning or just throw you into these episodes after completing the main ones is beyond me.

These Special Episodes also feature some of the coolest and most creative features and level design in the entire game, so PLEASE do yourself a favor and play these after you finish the main story. It's a shame that most people that play this game don't get to experience this.

Now about the actual game, wow. It's SO good. Not necessarily because of the gameplay, but because of pretty much everything else. The story and writing are fantastic, the level design and pacing are on point, the visuals are beautiful and have aged really well, the music and sound design are great, and the gameplay is pretty fun. 

I've seen a lot of people complain about combat in this game, but I actually quite like it. It's pretty unique, keeps the door open to a lot of creative and surprising opportunities and twists to the formula (especially during the Special Episodes), and feels pretty good. My only complaints would be about the dodging mechanic that does kinda suck, and a particular enemy type that teleports/runs around and is just straight up not fun to fight, but these don't show up that often.

The story here is the big star of the show, though. It’s SO good. From its presentation to the way it’s structured, it’s a masterclass in vídeo game writing. It keeps you interested and engaged during the entire game, doesn’t overstay its welcome, and knows perfectly when to throw scary moments, funny interactions and crazy twists at you. It’s filled with interesting and believeable characters you actually care about, has enough room for you to come to your own conclusions about a lot of things, and respects the player’s intelligence.

Like many people lately, I’ve picked this up because of Alan Wake 2. I’ve seen people say that you don’t really need to have played the other games before playing AW2, but I wholeheartedly disagree. Even if you can understand AW2 on its own, the journey you go on in AW1 will undoubtedly enhance your experience whenever you do get to AW2. Also, AW1 is just a great game on its own, and you should play it even if you never plan on getting AW2 (I mean, most people’s PCs can’t even run that anyway, but you can definitely run AW1 today). 

This game also takes A LOT of inspiration from Twin Peaks, and you will pick up on this very early on if you’ve seen the show. A ton of Alan Wake’s narrative, characters and world elements have been greatly inspired by David Lynch’s masterpiece, and this is a good thing in this case. The game wears this inspiration on its sleeve, but it never feels cheap or copied; they borrow a lot of things from there, but they do it in their own way, and it works beautifully. If you haven’t seen Twin Peaks, I would greatly suggest that you do watch it - all of the seasons - because it will greatly increase your appreciation for this game.

As a closing note, I think it’s worth mentioning that the game has a prequel miniseries called Bright Falls and it’s available in YouTube, and it’s pretty good.

Alan Wake is not a perfect game, but it is a very memorable one.

The core idea is simple. You fight darkness with light. It sounds basic, but it works surprisingly well and gives the combat its own identity. The real highlight, though, is the story. It feels like stepping into a psychological thriller, with a constant sense of mystery that keeps pulling you forward.
The early game is rough. The loop is repetitive, and most of the time, you are just running through forests, fighting the same enemies again and again. It can feel boring at first.
However, if you stick with it, the game gets much better.
As you progress, later chapters introduce new mechanics at a steady pace. Driving sections, poltergeist objects, chase sequences, and more variety in encounters keep things fresh. Chapters 4 and 5 are where everything clicks. Combat also becomes more fun once you unlock tools like flashbangs and flares, especially when dealing with groups.
There are still issues. Combat can feel clunky. Alan is slower than his enemies, so you are often forced to fight. Enemy spawns can be annoying too, especially when you get hit from outside your view.
Even with those flaws, the game delivers something special. Strong atmosphere, memorable characters, and a story that feels different from most games.

If you like Max Payne or enjoy the vibe of Stephen King stories, this is an easy pick.

Alan Wake is one of the most atmospheric and engaging psychological thriller games I have ever played. Developed by Remedy Entertainment, it follows the story of a bestselling writer, Alan Wake, who travels to the small town of Bright Falls with his wife to escape writer’s block. However, things quickly take a dark turn when his wife disappears, and he finds himself trapped in a supernatural nightmare, with shadowy enemies hunting him and pages of a manuscript he doesn’t remember writing coming to life.

The game’s biggest strength is its storytelling. Inspired by Stephen King and Twin Peaks, Alan Wake delivers a gripping narrative filled with mystery, psychological horror, and mind-bending twists. The episodic structure makes it feel like a TV series, keeping players hooked with cliffhangers and suspense. The game’s setting is equally impressive, with beautifully eerie environments, dense forests, and fog-covered roads that enhance the sense of isolation and fear.

Gameplay revolves around light-based combat, where players must use flashlights to weaken enemies before finishing them off with firearms. This unique mechanic adds tension, forcing players to manage batteries and ammo carefully. However, combat can become repetitive over time. Despite this, the excellent atmosphere, well-written characters, and haunting soundtrack make Alan Wake a memorable experience. It’s a must-play for fans of psychological horror and narrative-driven games.

Alan Wake, released back in 2010, is still one of the most unique games I’ve ever played. I just replayed it recently after last touching it in 2011, and honestly, it still holds up. The atmosphere, the light vs. dark mechanic, and the whole episodic story thing are pretty solid. It doesn’t feel like a typical horror game; it’s more like a thriller with a hefty dose of mystery. As a big Remedy fan who’s played all their games, I can say Alan Wake 2 (released in 2023) is easily one of the best games I’ve played in a long time. They really knocked it out of the park.

The one downside to the first game? Combat can get repetitive. I mean, how many times can you shine a flashlight at someone before it gets old? But honestly, the world, story, and overall vibe more than make up for it. Also, RIP James McCaffrey. He voiced Thomas Zane in Alan Wake and really brought something special to the role. His legacy with Remedy, especially as Max Payne, will never be forgotten. And seriously, I just wish Alan Wake 2 would get released on Steam at some point. It really deserves to be there too.

If I were to judge solely based on my first impression I would say that Alan Wake is an absolutely unique game. Featuring not only a captivating story and stunning audiovisual presentation but also an incredible atmosphere. Unfortunately the longer I spent in the town of Bright Falls the more I began to feel fatigued. The enjoyment of the shooter was ultimately overshadowed by its biggest flaw – a monotonous and dull gameplay experience. Alan Wake’s world is full of references to contemporary pop culture. In addition to the most obvious nods to Stephen King's work the game also includes elements inspired by TV series and direct references to Remedy's previous hit – the Max Payne series.

Alan Wake is a very interesting game with a very interesting storyline and way of storytelling.
